_Paenitentiam Agere_ (“To Do Penance”) is the encyclical of Pope John XXIII issued on July 1, 1962, three months before he opened the Second Vatican Council. He asks the whole Church — clergy and laity — to prepare for the Council by prayer, interior repentance, and outward penance.

## 1. What is Paenitentiam Agere?
_Paenitentiam Agere_ is a papal encyclical on the need for interior and exterior penance. John had already warned, when he formally convoked the Council, that prayer and virtue should include voluntary mortification. This letter dwells on that request at length. He wants the Council’s work to fall on souls that are ready.

## 2. Why penance before a council?
Because, he writes, God does not draw near in a solemn way without first calling his people to prayer and penance. Moses, the prophets, John the Baptist, and Jesus himself begin with conversion: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” A council reaffirms God’s rights and mankind’s duties. That work asks a clean heart, not only a full agenda.

## 3. What is interior penance?
Detestation of sin and a firm purpose of amendment. John names the ordinary means: a good confession, participation in the Eucharistic Sacrifice, and Holy Communion. Outward acts, he says, are useless unless they come with a clear conscience. The sacrament of penance restores the baptismal robe that sin has stained. He quotes Trent’s hard and hopeful phrase: the Fathers called penance a laborious kind of baptism.

## 4. What is exterior penance?
Two layers. First, accepting the sorrows, inconveniences, and duties of daily life in union with Christ — the penance nobody chooses and everybody has. Second, voluntary acts: fasting, self-denial, almsgiving, works of mercy, offered freely. He points to St. Paul chastising his body, and to the saints whose mortification puts comfortable Christians to shame. The aim is love, a share in what is lacking in Christ’s sufferings for the sake of his body, the Church.

## 5. What practical steps does he ask?
A solemn novena to the Holy Spirit in every parish immediately before the Council, to beg light for the Council Fathers, with a plenary indulgence under the usual conditions. He also suggests a public act of prayer and propitiation in each diocese, with sermons inviting the faithful to mercy and penance. He asks priests, religious, children, the sick, and the afflicted to lead the way.

## 6. Does he appeal to earlier councils?
Yes. Innocent III asked prayer, fasting, and almsgiving before the Fourth Lateran Council. Gregory X ordered a fast before the Second Council of Lyons. Pius IX told the faithful to prepare for the First Vatican Council by ridding their souls of sin. John XXIII places Vatican II in that sequence. A council is a gift that a praying Church knows how to receive.

## 7. Is the tone severe?
It is serious, and it is a father’s seriousness. He says plainly that he will not threaten or abuse the Church’s forgetful children. He appeals. He also refuses the modern habit of chasing pleasure until the nobler powers of the soul go soft. Penance, in this letter, is how Christians stay awake.

## 8. What fruit does he hope for?
A reinvigorated faith, love, and moral life among Catholics, and — he adds with the hope that runs through his pontificate — a sincerity that will draw separated Christians toward the one flock. He also hopes that when the bishops arrive in Rome they will come “laden with spiritual riches,” the prayer and self-denial of their people. The Council’s seed, he says, must not fall on the path.

## 9. Why does it still matter?
Vatican II is often remembered for windows opened and documents signed. _Paenitentiam Agere_ remembers the condition John XXIII set beforehand: renewal begins in repentance. Any reading of the Council that skips conversion has skipped the pope who called it. The same pastor wrote _Pacem in Terris_ the following Holy Thursday, already dying, on peace for the whole human family.

## 10. Where can I read it?
The English text is on the Vatican website.

## Death of Pope John XXIII
3/6/2023
Pope John XXIII
* * *
Exactly sixty years ago, on June 3rd 1963, Pope John XXIII died.
Cardinal Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli was elected pope on October 28th 1958, at the age of seventy-six.
​Pope John XXIII explained his choice of name to the cardinals: 'I will be called John... a name sweet to us, because it is the name of our father, dear to us because it is the name of the humble parish church where we were baptised, the solemn name of numberless cathedrals scattered throughout the world, including our own basilica (St. John Lateran).Twenty-two Johns of indisputable legitimacy have been pope, and almost all had a brief pontificate. We have preferred to hide the smallness of our name behind this magnificent succession of Roman Pontiffs'. *
_Il Papa Buono_, as he came to be popularly known, has gone down in history for convening the Second Vatican Council, the first session of which opened on October 11th 1962.
John XXIII (r. 1958-63) was beatified by Pope John Paul II on September 3rd 2000. Fourteen years later he was canonised by Pope Francis.
The feast day of Pope John XXIII is October 11th.
*There had, in fact, only been twenty-one Johns 'of indi sputable legitimacy', as there had never been a Pope John XX.

# On This Day in Rome: June 3rd 1963: Death of Pope John XXIII - Walks in Rome (Est. 2001)
## Death of Pope John XXIII
3/6/2023
Pope John XXIII
* * *
Exactly sixty years ago, on June 3rd 1963, Pope John XXIII died.
Cardinal Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli was elected pope on October 28th 1958, at the age of seventy-six.
​Pope John XXIII explained his choice of name to the cardinals: 'I will be called John... a name sweet to us, because it is the name of our father, dear to us because it is the name of the humble parish church where we were baptised, the solemn name of numberless cathedrals scattered throughout the world, including our own basilica (St. John Lateran).Twenty-two Johns of indisputable legitimacy have been pope, and almost all had a brief pontificate. We have preferred to hide the smallness of our name behind this magnificent succession of Roman Pontiffs'. *
_Il Papa Buono_, as he came to be popularly known, has gone down in history for convening the Second Vatican Council, the first session of which opened on October 11th 1962.
John XXIII (r. 1958-63) was beatified by Pope John Paul II on September 3rd 2000. Fourteen years later he was canonised by Pope Francis.
The feast day of Pope John XXIII is October 11th.
*There had, in fact, only been twenty-one Johns 'of indi sputable legitimacy', as there had never been a Pope John XX.

**Pope John XXIII**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXIII#cite_note-8) (born **Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli**;[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXIII#cite_note-9) 25 November 1881–3 June 1963) was head of the Catholic Church and sovereign of Vatican City from 28 October 1958 until his death on 3 June 1963.
Roncalli was among 13 children born to Marianna Mazzola and Giovanni Battista Roncalli in a family of sharecroppers who lived in Sotto il Monte, a village in the province of Bergamo, Lombardy.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXIII#cite_note-saints-10) He was ordained to the priesthood on 10 August 1904 and served in a number of posts, as nuncio in France and a delegate to Bulgaria, Greece and Turkey. In a consistory on 12 January 1953 Pope Pius XII made Roncalli a cardinal as the Cardinal-priest of Santa Prisca in addition to naming him as the Patriarch of Venice. Roncalli was unexpectedly elected pope on 28 October 1958 at age 76 after Pope Pius XII's death. Pope John XXIII surprised those who expected him to be a caretaker pope by calling the historic Second Vatican Council (1962–1965), the first session opening on 11 October 1962, which is now his feast.

John XXIII made many passionate speeches during his pontificate. His views on equality were summed up in his statement, "We were all made in God's image, and thus, we are all Godly alike."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXIII#cite_note-11)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXIII#cite_note-12) He made a major impact on the Catholic Church, opening it up to the changes of the Second Vatican Council and by his own dealings with other churches and nations. In Italian politics, he prohibited bishops from interfering with local elections, and he helped the Christian Democracy party to cooperate with the Italian Socialist Party. In international affairs, his _Ostpolitik_ engaged in dialogue with the communist countries of Eastern Europe. He especially reached out to the Eastern Orthodox churches.
John XXIII's overall goal was to modernize the Church by emphasizing its pastoral role, and its necessary involvement with affairs of state. He dropped the traditional rule of 70 cardinals, increasing the number to 85. He used the opportunity to name the first cardinals from Africa, Japan, and the Philippines. He promoted ecumenical movements in cooperation with other Christian faiths. In doctrinal matters, he ended the practice of automatically formulating social and political policies on the basis of old theological propositions.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXIII#cite_note-13)

John XXIII did not live to see the Second Vatican Council to completion. He was diagnosed with stomach cancer in September 1962 and died on 3 June 1963. His cause for canonization was opened on 18 November 1965 by his successor, Pope Paul VI, who declared him a Servant of God. He was beatified by Pope John Paul II in 2000. On 5 July 2013, Pope Francis, bypassing the traditionally required second miracle, declared John XXIII a saint based on his virtuous lifestyle and because of the good that came from his opening of the Second Vatican Council. Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli was born on 25 November 1881 in Sotto il Monte, a small country village in the Bergamo province of the Lombardy region of Italy. He was the eldest son of Giovanni Battista Roncalli and his wife Marianna Giulia Mazzola, and fourth in a family of thirteen.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXIII#cite_note-16)
Roncalli's family, c.1890
His family worked as sharecroppers, as did most of the people of Sotto il Monte – a striking contrast to that of his predecessor, Eugenio Pacelli (Pope Pius XII), who came from a family established in senior roles in the Papal administration. The Roncallis maintained a vineyard and cornfields and kept cattle.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXIII#cite_note-18)

In 1889, Roncalli received both his First Communion and Confirmation at the age of 8.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXIII#cite_note-19)

After this, he returned to his town to celebrate Mass for feast of the Assumption.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXIII#cite_note-22)

In 1905, Giacomo Radini-Tedeschi, the new Bishop of Bergamo, appointed Roncalli as his secretary. Roncalli worked for Radini-Tedeschi until the bishop's death on 22 August 1914, two days after the death of Pius X. Radini-Tedeschi's last words to Roncalli were "Angelo, pray for peace". After their meeting, Pope Benedict XV appointed him as the Italian president of the Society for the Propagation of the Faith. Roncalli was among 13 children born to Marianna Mazzola and Giovanni Battista Roncalli in a family of sharecroppers who lived in Sotto il Monte, a village in the province of Bergamo, Lombardy.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXIII#cite_note-saints-10) He was ordained to the priesthood on 10 August 1904 and served in a number of posts, as nuncio in France and a delegate to Bulgaria, Greece and Turkey. In a consistory on 12 January 1953 Pope Pius XII made Roncalli a cardinal as the Cardinal-priest of Santa Prisca in addition to naming him as the Patriarch of Venice. Roncalli was unexpectedly elected pope on 28 October 1958 at age 76 after Pope Pius XII's death. Pope John XXIII surprised those who expected him to be a caretaker pope by calling the historic Second Vatican Council (1962–1965), the first session opening on 11 October 1962, which is now his feast.

In international affairs, his _Ostpolitik_ engaged in dialogue with the communist countries of Eastern Europe. He especially reached out to the Eastern Orthodox churches.
John XXIII's overall goal was to modernize the Church by emphasizing its pastoral role, and its necessary involvement with affairs of state. He dropped the traditional rule of 70 cardinals, increasing the number to 85. He used the opportunity to name the first cardinals from Africa, Japan, and the Philippines. He promoted ecumenical movements in cooperation with other Christian faiths. In doctrinal matters, he ended the practice of automatically formulating social and political policies on the basis of old theological propositions.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXIII#cite_note-13)

They ask: When did the place of death of Paenitentiam Agere's author become its own country? The author is Pope John XXIII. His place of death: Apostolic Palace, Vatican City. They ask when did that place become its own country. So we're asked: when did Vatican City become an independent sovereign state? That happened when the Lateran Treaty established Vatican City as a sovereign state in 1929 (1929 Vatican City State established by Lateran Treaty signed on 11 February 1929). But might be earlier? Vatican City became a sovereign state in 1929 after Lateran Treaty. So answer: 1929 (specifically 11 February 1929). Provide context.
steps.text:
Paenitentiam Agere was written by Pope **John XXIII** (born Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli).  He died in his apartment in the **Apostolic Palace at Vatican City** on 3 June 1963.  

The **place of his death**—Vatican City—was not an independent country until the **Lateran Treaty** was signed on **11 February 1929**, which established Vatican City as a sovereign state.  Thus, Vatican City became its own country in 1929.
